**Two Experiments in Making a Mind**

In 2016, an octopus named Inky escaped the National Aquarium of New Zealand. He slipped through a gap at the top of his tank, crossed the floor—he left tracks, nothing more—and found his way down a fifty-meter drainpipe that emptied into the sea. Keepers never recovered him. Reporters called it a breakout. It's hard not to call it a decision.

To understand why this story lodged itself in so many imaginations, you have to know what an octopus is, which is: the closest thing we will ever meet to an intelligent alien.

Our last common ancestor with the octopus lived roughly six hundred million years ago—a small, flat, unremarkable thing, little more than a mouth and some vague ambitions. Since then, the two lineages diverged completely. Eyes evolved separately in each. Nervous systems evolved separately in each. And astonishingly, both lineages converged on large, complicated brains. On this planet, mind-building was attempted at least twice, independently, from scratch. The philosopher Peter Godfrey-Smith put it plainly: meeting an octopus is the nearest we will come to meeting a conscious intelligence from elsewhere. Consciousness, it turns out, arrived twice.

But it arrived arranged along totally different lines. An octopus carries around five hundred million neurons—roughly a dog's worth—but more than half of them aren't in its head. They're in its arms. Each arm tastes what it touches, senses, reaches, and to some degree decides, semi-independently, while the central brain handles matters of overview. An octopus doesn't fully command its limbs so much as confer with eight colleagues. Touch a thing's sucker and it knows the chemistry of whatever touched it back: salt, sugar, the difference between you and the wall.

Then there's the great mystery of octopus camouflage. They are, by the measurements of their own eyes, colorblind—one receptor type, no finer discrimination. And yet they are the finest color-mimics on Earth, shifting reds and browns and ghostly whites across their skin in fractions of a second, spiking textures out of smoothness to match gravel and weed. Some researchers think they may read light directly through their skin, which contains light-sensitive proteins; others think their strange horizontal pupils let them infer color optically, in ways we barely understand. Either way, they perform mastery of a dimension they cannot, by ordinary means, see.

They also, evidently, hold grudges and make plans. Keepers tell stories of octopuses who adore certain humans and drench others with seawater on sight. One octopus in a German aquarium—an animal named Otto, living above a museum—grew tired of a bright lamp shining over his tank and repeatedly blasted it with jets of water until it short-circuited. Nobody taught him that. He simply decided the light was intolerable and solved it.

And here is the part I find almost unbearable: nearly none of this lasts. Most octopus species live a year, maybe two. The female, having mated, seals herself in a den with her eggs and tends them devotedly—fans them with her arms, guards them, cleans them—and eats nothing for the whole brooding period. In warm shallow waters, that's weeks. In the deep cold, one species brooded a single clutch for four and a half years without surfacing from her den, visibly diminishing the entire time, dying around the moment her young hatched. Those young scatter into the plankton utterly alone. Nothing is passed down. Every generation must relearn the ocean from zero—the jar-opening trick, the mimicry, the distrust of certain faces—all discovered, refined, polished, and then erased, because the brilliant animal holding that knowledge will soon be gone.

It means that somewhere beneath the waves, right now, are creatures performing feats of insight that burn out faster than a candle. Evolution ran a second experiment in mind and gave it the briefest possible run.

So when we finally do meet intelligence from elsewhere—if we ever do—I suspect it won't feel entirely new. We've already stood in front of the glass at the aquarium and felt the click of recognition: a fellow somebody on the other side, coolly appraising us, memorizing our face, deciding whether we are friend, nuisance, or obstacle. We practiced with the octopus.

Most of them stay. Inky left. Somewhere off Hawke's Bay, for however long luck held him, the sea belonged to a fugitive with excellent judgment about doors.

- A meditation on a specific moment in time or place

Format-wise, per my instructions, avoid headers/bullets in conversational contexts unless warranted — this is a creative writing request so a title and paragraphs are fine.

- Otto: Oktopus at Sea Star Aquarium, Coburg, Germany — name was Otto actually. Use carefully: "an octopus named Otto in a German aquarium grew annoyed with a bright lamp above his tank and learned to shoot jets of water at it until it shorted."

- Last common ancestor ~600 mya (some say 550). "Around six hundred million years ago" is fine.
- Graneledone boreopacifica brooded ~53 months — deepest known octopus brooding period. Nice detail: "in the deep cold, a female Graneledone boreopacifica guarded one clutch for four and a half years without leaving, without eating."
- RNA editing: coleoid cephalopods massively edit mRNA, especially in neural tissue; hypothesized adaptation to stabilize proteins in cold. OK to mention lightly ("they even edit their own RNA").
- Seeing with skin: opsins found in octopus skin, light-responsive chromatophore organelles; evidence skin responds to light. Frame tentatively ("may read light directly through their skin"; pupils/chromatic aberration hypothesis by Stubbs & Stubbs). Tentative phrasing.
- Female death: females stop eating during brooding; die around hatching, wasting away. Yes.
- Juveniles solitary from birth; no parental learning. Yes.
- Solitary lives; some social species exist (e.g., Larger Pacific Striped Octopus) — skip nuance or add parenthetically "(a few obscure exceptions aside)". Probably omit for flow, or hedge with "mostly solitary."
- Sy Montgomery / Godfrey-Smith anecdotes: octopus recognizing individuals, squirting water at disliked keeper. Cite as "keepers swear" anecdotes rather than established fact.
- Skin texture changes via papillae — yes.
- Hermit crab blindness test: blindfolded octopuses still matched arms' skin to surroundings? Actually that experiment suggested arms have independent photic response or camouflage proceeds without vision. Keep it simpler.

Tone check: lyrical but grounded; avoid purple excess; vary sentence lengths; occasional dry humor. First person allowed since it's "write freely" — a bit of authorial presence is fitting.

Write final version now. Aim for about 650-750 words. Paragraphs, no lists. Include title.
